**February 29, 1960 — A Monday**

Before anything else: you were born on a day that does not exist in three out of every four years. February 29 comes around only when the calendar corrects itself against the actual length of Earth's orbit — a correction the Romans first codified, that Julius Caesar formalized, and that the Gregorian reform refined. In sixty-six years of life you have had sixteen birthdays on the actual date. You share this with a remarkably small fraternity. The rarity of the day is worth sitting with before anything else.

---

**On the exact day you were born, a city was destroyed.**

Late in the evening of February 29, 1960 — local time, while much of Morocco slept — an earthquake struck Agadir. The magnitude was not extreme by seismic standards, but the fault was shallow, the buildings were not built for it, and the destruction was catastrophic. Roughly 12,000 to 15,000 people died, approximately a third of the city's entire population. Agadir was essentially leveled. The international rescue response that followed was one of the early examples of modern disaster relief — military units, Red Cross teams, and journalists all arriving within days. The city was eventually rebuilt from scratch, on a different urban plan, at a different location. The old Agadir no longer exists. It happened the night you were born.

---

**The day before your birth, the Olympics closed.**

The 1960 Winter Games at Squaw Valley, California — the first Winter Olympics ever held in the United States — concluded on February 28, the day before you arrived. These were also the first Olympics broadcast live on television, and the first at which a computer was used to tabulate results. Walt Disney had organized the opening ceremonies. The Soviet Union led the medal count. The Cold War competition that pervaded every aspect of international life in 1960 played out on the ski slopes and speed skating rinks of the Sierra Nevada, with American audiences watching for the first time in their living rooms rather than reading about it the next morning. The Games ended. You began.

---

**A sit-in was four weeks old and spreading.**

On February 1, 1960 — twenty-eight days before your birth — four Black college students sat down at the whites-only lunch counter at a Woolworth's in Greensboro, North Carolina, ordered coffee, and refused to leave when told they could not be served. By February 29, the sit-in movement had spread to dozens of cities across the South. The students were trained in nonviolent resistance; they sat quietly while people poured food on them and screamed in their faces. The tactic was working. Within months it would compel desegregation at lunch counters across the region. You were born twenty-eight days into one of the most effective tactical innovations in American civil rights history.

---

**Three weeks after your birth, Sharpeville.**

On March 21, 1960 — less than a month after you were born — South African police opened fire on a crowd of Black protesters at Sharpeville, killing 69 people, most of them shot in the back. The Sharpeville Massacre marked a decisive turn: the African National Congress was banned, Nelson Mandela and others concluded that nonviolent protest alone could not work against the apartheid regime, and the armed resistance phase of the struggle began. The world's response — condemnation, sanctions, moral pressure — would take decades to accumulate into change. The apartheid system that hardened in the weeks after your birth would not end until you were in your thirties.

---

**Nineteen sixty was a year in motion.**

The year you were born is sometimes called a pivot year. Kennedy would defeat Nixon in November, the narrowest popular-vote margin in decades, and a new political generation would arrive in Washington. Seventeen African nations gained independence in 1960 alone — more than in any year before or since — in what became known as the Year of Africa. The oral contraceptive pill received FDA approval in May, beginning one of the most consequential social transformations of the century. The laser was first successfully operated. Cassius Clay — not yet Muhammad Ali — won a gold medal in boxing at the Rome Summer Olympics in August. The world was moving with unusual speed.

---

**The arc of a lifetime**

You are 66. You have had sixteen birthdays on the actual date.

You were three when Kennedy was assassinated — too young to remember it clearly, young enough that it is part of the atmosphere of your earliest childhood. You were eight in 1968, a year when two assassinations, a war, and a political convention in chaos compressed themselves into twelve months. You were nine when Apollo 11 landed on the moon, and that belongs to you in the way it belongs to everyone who was old enough to watch it live.

You came of age in the 1970s — Watergate, stagflation, the end of the Vietnam War, the oil shock. You were in your mid-twenties when the AIDS epidemic began its quiet emergence and then its devastating public presence. You were 29 when the Berlin Wall came down, the same age that Nasser was when he joined the coup that would eventually make him president. The Soviet Union dissolved when you were 31.

You were 41 on September 11, 2001. The smartphone arrived in your late forties. The pandemic at 60.

The Agadir that was destroyed on your birthday has been rebuilt and is a functioning city of several hundred thousand people now. Morocco has changed enormously. The Woolworth's chain that maintained a segregated lunch counter when you were born went out of business in 1997.

---

**What kind of world**

The Monday morning of February 29, 1960 was still a world of rotary phones and physical maps, of airline travel as luxury, of television as a recent and slightly astonishing domestic presence. A world where a computer that fit in a room was state of the art. Where the vast majority of sub-Saharan Africa was still under European colonial administration. Where the nuclear arsenals were real but the doctrine for managing them was still being invented.

The rarity of your birthday is a useful frame: February 29 requires the entire system to be working correctly, the calendar and the orbit in precise coordination, the correction applied. You arrived on the correction day. Sixty-six years later, the world that required correcting has been revised in ways no one in that delivery room could have begun to predict.
